How to use Price Truth

A step-by-step walkthrough of every page, every button and every number in the dashboard — what it means, where it comes from, and how far you can trust it.

8 pagesReal screenshotsEvery verdict explainedGlossary of terms

1Opening the app

Price Truth runs in any web browser — desktop, tablet or phone. No account or installation is needed to use it.

On this computer

Start the app, then open http://localhost:8501.

On another device on the same Wi-Fi

Open http://<computer's Wi-Fi IP>:8501, for example http://192.168.1.216:8501.

Online

Once deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud, open the public …streamlit.app link.

Starting the app yourself (for developers)

From the project folder run:

.venv/bin/python -m streamlit run app.py

Setup for a fresh computer is in README.md. The first price check after start-up can take about a second while the model warms up; later checks are faster.

2How results are shown

Every page uses the same visual language, so once you know it you can read any result at a glance.

Verdict banners

The main answer always appears in a coloured banner. The icon and the title carry the meaning, so it is clear even without colour.

LookMeaningExample
✓ GreenGood for you as a buyer“Lower than expected”, “A real price drop”, “Option 2 is the best value”
≈ PurpleNormal, nothing unusual“In line with similar listings”, “A usual discount, not a special deal”
! RedA warning sign“Higher than expected”, “The discount looks inflated”, “Same price, smaller pack”
i GreyNot enough information for a verdict — the app explains why instead of guessing“Not enough comparable listings”, “No forecast: last price is as good”

Source labels

Small labels next to results tell you where the data came from:

LabelMeaning
Historical catalogueA real Amazon (January 2023) or Flipkart (2015–16) listing. Not a live offer.
Live responseFetched just now from Open Food Facts.
Saved responseA copy saved earlier, shown with its date — used offline or when the live service fails.
Your entryData you typed or uploaded yourself.
Published reportTaken from a cited news report (shrinkflation cases).
Empty states are answers tooWhen there is nothing to show — no search matches, too little history — the app says why and what to try next, instead of showing an empty chart or a made-up number.

3Home & navigation

The home page is the quickest way in: type what you are buying and press Check price.

  1. Search. Type a product such as “smart watch” and press Check price. You land on the Price check page with your search filled in.
  2. Headline numbers. How many listings the app knows (21,267), the model's typical error on products it never saw (about 21%), how many dated shop prices it holds, and how many shopping platforms it compares.
  3. Tool cards. Click any card to jump to that tool. “How Price Truth works” gives a three-line summary.
PageUse it to…
Price checkJudge a price and a discount, see its history and where it is cheaper
Unit priceFind the best-value pack size
Food & packsLook up a barcode and its shop prices
ShrinkflationSee packs that shrank at the same price
My observationsTrack prices you have seen yourself
CatalogueBrowse and download all listings

On a phone, the sidebar is hidden — tap the » arrow at the top left to open it.

4Price check

The main tool. Pick a product, enter the price you see, and get a verdict with its reasons, a discount check, the price history and the cheapest place to buy.

Step 1 — Find and choose the product

  1. Search historical listings. Type a few words (e.g. “smart watch”). Fewer, simpler words find more matches.
  2. Platform. Choose Both, Amazon or Flipkart.
  3. Click a row in the results table to choose it. The table shows the catalogue prices on the date the data was collected, plus the Variant (colour, model code) and ID so that similar-looking listings can be told apart.
  4. Check the product card. It confirms exactly which product you picked: platform, category, variant, ID, currency and the date it was observed.

Step 2 — Enter the price and check it

BoxWhat to enter
Listed (MRP) priceThe crossed-out “was” price or MRP the seller shows. The advertised discount is worked out from this.
Price you were offeredThe price you would actually pay.

Both boxes start at today's price for the listing. Change them to what you see in the shop or app, then press Check this price.

Step 3 — Read the verdict

ItemMeaning
Verdict bannerWhether your price is lower than, in line with or higher than what similar listings sold for. See every verdict.
Advertised discountHow much off MRP the seller claims: 1 − price ÷ MRP.
Model estimateWhat a trained model expects similar listings to sell for.
Expected rangeThe band that contains 90% of real selling prices for comparable products in testing. It is not a 90% chance that a discount is real.
Range chartPurple band = expected range, purple line = estimate, red diamond = your price. Left of the band is cheap; right of it is expensive.

Step 4 — See why, and save the result

Each bar shows how much one factor raised (purple, right) or lowered (coral, left) the expected price, in percent, starting from a typical listing. For example, a high MRP usually raises the estimate; a low-priced category lowers it. These are computed by SHAP, a standard method for explaining a model's output.

What this chart is notIt explains the model's estimate. It does not show whether a seller is honest.
  • Comparable listings: how many training listings share this platform and subcategory. Below 30, the app shows the estimate without a verdict.
  • Download PDF report / data (JSON): saves the result. Open on Amazon/Flipkart opens the original listing.

When to be careful — reliability warning

For a few product groups the model is less accurate in testing (for example Flipkart Electronics). A yellow warning then appears with the measured accuracy. Treat the verdict as a rough guide there.

4a · Discount check tab

Is the advertised discount a real saving, or is it inflated?

NumberMeaning
Advertised discountThe discount the seller claims, against MRP.
Usual discount (90 days)The typical discount this product showed over the last 90 days.
Lowest price, 30 daysThe lowest price in the 30 days before the current offer (before the sale began, if a sale is on). This is the fair “was” price.
Real saving vs 30-day lowHow much you really save compared with that lowest price. Negative means you pay more than the recent low.
The rule behind “inflated”A discount is flagged when it is advertised as at least 5 points bigger than usual while the price is less than 5% below its lowest price in the 30 days before the promotion. This follows the EU's “30-day lowest price” rule for sale prices, adapted to Indian MRP-based listings. It catches the common trick of raising the MRP or the price just before a sale.

Model estimate. Below the rule, a second check estimates the risk from the listing alone (price, MRP, discount size, category, platform, rating and whether a sale is on), with a chart of what raised or lowered the risk. A listing is flagged at about 17% risk or more. The rule above is the stronger signal, because it uses the price history.

Try itRaise the MRP box well above normal and check again — you will see the inflated verdict.

4b · Price history & timing tab

Is now a good time to buy?

  1. Chart. The purple line is the selling price; shaded bands are sale events (Prime Day, Big Billion Days…); the dashed red line is your price. The MRP line is hidden when it is far above the price — click “Listed (MRP)” in the legend to show it.
  2. Timing verdict. Compares your price with the last 90 days: Below the usual price (cheaper than 75% of recent days), Around the usual price, or Above the usual price.
  3. Usual (median) price is the middle price of recent days; Your quote vs median is how far above or below it you are.
  4. Next sale. The next announced sale on that platform. Prices sometimes rise just before a sale, so compare with the 30-day low.
  5. Tomorrow's price. A next-day forecast is shown only if it beats simply repeating today's price on past days. Online prices change rarely, so often the honest answer is “No forecast: last price is as good”.

4c · Where to buy tab

The same product across Indian platforms, ranked by what you would actually pay.

  • The banner names the cheapest platform including delivery and platform fees, and how much you save.
  • Each row shows the price, delivery and fees (e.g. Amazon ₹40 delivery under ₹499 plus a ₹5 fee; Flipkart ₹40 under ₹500 plus ₹3; Myntra ₹99 under ₹1,000), and a Search button that opens that platform's search for the product. “Out of stock” rows are listed last.
  • Only platforms that sell the product's category appear (for example Croma and Reliance Digital for electronics; Myntra and Ajio for fashion).

5Unit price

Which pack size is really cheaper? Compare 2 to 4 options on price per 100 g, 100 ml or per item.

  1. Choose the currency and how many options (2, 3 or 4).
  2. For each option enter the price, the quantity per pack, the unit (g, kg, ml, l or count) and the number of packs (for multipacks).
  3. Press Compare value. The banner names the best value and how much cheaper it is per unit than the most expensive option; the chart and table rank all options.
Good to knowKilograms and grams (or litres and millilitres) are converted automatically. Mixing weight with volume or items is refused, because they cannot be compared.

6Food & packs

Look up a packaged food by name or barcode, check its pack size, and see what shops charged on which dates.

Pack details

  1. Type a name (e.g. “Maggi”) or an 8–14 digit barcode and press Search. Switch on Saved responses only to work offline with saved data.
  2. Pick the product from the list. The card shows brand, pack size, barcode and where it is sold, with the source and date (Open Food Facts).
  3. Compare this pack's value sends the pack size straight to the Unit price page — just add its price there. View source record opens the original data.

Price history

  1. Pick a store, currency and price basis. The list shows how many prices each store has, longest history first.
  2. Read the chart, then type your current price and press Compare with history for a below / around / above usual verdict.
  3. Refresh prices fetches the latest observations for this barcode (needs internet). Source observations lists every row with a link to its source.
“Price basis unknown”Some shop reports do not say whether a price is per item or per kilogram. The app then refuses to compare a quote rather than risk a wrong answer.

Long-history example

7Shrinkflation

“Same price, smaller pack.” See how much more you really pay when a pack shrinks.

  1. Choose a product. Cited cases include Vim, Haldiram's, Parle-G and seven Maggi pack sizes; generic examples show multi-step shrinkage.
  2. Quantity reduction: how much smaller the pack got. Hidden price increase: how much the price per gram (or ml) rose, even though the label price did not change.
  3. Read About this case and open Read the original report to check the source.
Example52 g → 48 g at ₹10 is 7.7% less food, which is an 8.3% higher price per gram.

8My observations

Record prices you see yourself — from receipts, shop shelves or apps — and analyse them. Your data stays in your browser session and is never used to train the models.

Add or import

  1. Add one observation: fill in the product ID or barcode, name, variant, store, currency, date, total price, total quantity and unit, and an HTTPS link to your evidence (receipt photo, shop page). Press Add to my session observations.
  2. Or import a CSV (UTF-8, up to 2 MB). Download the CSV template for the exact columns.
  3. Save my observations downloads your data as CSV — do this before closing, because the session is cleared when you leave. Clear session observations deletes everything.
CSV columnExampleNotes
product_id8901725118921Barcode or any stable ID; leading zeros are kept
nameAashirvaad atta
variantwhole wheatFlavour, model or colour
storeCorner Store
currencyINRThree capital letters
date2026-10-07YYYY-MM-DD, not in the future
price245Total price paid
quantity5Total quantity bought at that price
unitkgg, kg, ml, l or count
source_urlhttps://…HTTPS link to your evidence

If any row is invalid, nothing is imported and the error says which problem to fix — so you never end up with half a file.

Price history & forecast

Choose the product, variant, store, currency and exact pack size. The forecast needs at least 40 consecutive days ending today or yesterday; it is shown only if it beats “same as the last price” on the most recent 10 days. Otherwise the app explains why (for example, “12 of 40 consecutive daily observations” with a progress bar).

Compare stores

Ranks stores by your quotes from today or yesterday for one product and pack size. Tick the box to confirm the packs and conditions (tax, delivery, membership) are the same. Rank 1 is the cheapest of your quotes — not a guarantee of the lowest price anywhere.

Pack changes

Choose one product at one store, confirm the records track the same variant over time, and press Analyse pack-size changes. Each row shows when the pack got smaller, by how much, and how much the price per unit rose.

9Catalogue

Browse all 21,267 Amazon and Flipkart listings and download any search as CSV.

Similar names can be different products or variants, so the catalogue never claims two listings are the same item. Prices are as recorded on the collection date.

10Methods & data

How accurate the app is, where the data comes from, and what it cannot do.

NumberMeaning
Held-out listings4,269 products kept aside and never used for training — the accuracy is measured on these.
Typical errorFor half of those products the estimate was within about 21% of the real price.
Mean absolute errorThe average gap between estimate and real price, in rupees.
R²How much of the variation in prices the model explains, from 0 (nothing) to 1 (everything). 0.96 overall.
ReliabilityGood R² ≥ 0.8 · Moderate 0.5–0.8 · Weak below 0.5 (a warning appears on the Price check).
Real and simulated dataThe product listings, food lookups, shop prices and cited shrinkflation cases are real. Daily price histories, cross-platform offers and the discount-model training labels are simulated — calibrated to published research on Indian sale calendars, discount depths and pricing — because no public source provides them. Every simulated row is marked provenance = synthetic in the data files. The price-estimate model is trained on real listings only.

11On your phone

Every page works on a phone. Columns stack vertically and the sidebar folds away.

Tap » at the top left to open the page list. Wide tables can be scrolled sideways with a finger.

12Every verdict explained

All the answers the app can give, and exactly when each appears.

Price check

VerdictWhen it appears
✓ Lower than expectedYour price is below the expected range. A good price by historical standards.
≈ In line with similar listingsYour price is inside the expected range.
! Higher than expectedYour price is above the range. The advertised discount may overstate the saving.
i Not enough comparable listingsFewer than 30 similar listings, so only the estimate is shown.

Discount check

VerdictWhen it appears
✓ A real price dropThe price is at least 5% below its lowest price of the previous 30 days.
≈ A usual discount, not a special dealThe discount is normal for this product and the price has not really dropped.
! The discount looks inflatedThe discount is advertised as 5+ points bigger than usual, but the price is not 5% below the pre-promotion 30-day low.

Buy timing (history)

VerdictWhen it appears
✓ Below the usual priceYour price is cheaper than three-quarters of recent prices.
≈ Around the usual priceWithin the middle half of recent prices.
! Above the usual priceDearer than three-quarters of recent prices.
i Not enough history yetFewer than 5 earlier dates.
i History too thin for a signalHistory older than 90 days or covering fewer than 14 days.

Next-day forecast

VerdictWhen it appears
✓ Forecast availableA method beat “same as last price” on the last 10 days; the estimate and its test error are shown.
i No forecast: last price is as goodNothing beat simply repeating the last price.
i Not enough history yetFewer than 40 daily observations.
i Gaps in the historyDays are missing; the app never fills gaps with guesses.
i History is out of dateThe latest observation is older than yesterday.
! History cannot be usedDuplicate dates or invalid prices.

13Glossary

Every term used in the app, in plain language.

MRP / listed price
The maximum retail price or “was” price the seller shows, usually crossed out.
Selling price
The price actually charged.
Advertised discount
1 − selling price ÷ MRP, as a percentage.
Usual discount
The product's typical (median) discount over the previous 90 days.
30-day low
The lowest price in the 30 days before the current offer or sale — the fair reference for “was” prices under the EU rule.
Real saving
How much the price is below the 30-day low. Negative means you pay more than the recent low.
Inflated discount
A discount that looks bigger than usual without a real price drop, often from raising the MRP or the price before a sale.
Model estimate
What the trained model expects similar listings to sell for, from MRP, rating, platform and category.
Expected range
A band calibrated to contain 90% of real selling prices for comparable products in testing.
SHAP / “What moved the estimate”
A standard method that splits a model's estimate into the push from each factor.
Comparable listings
Training listings on the same platform and in the same subcategory.
Risk score
The discount model's estimated chance that a discount is inflated, judged from the listing alone. Flagged at about 17%.
Median
The middle value: half the prices are lower, half are higher.
Quartile
The 25% and 75% points of recent prices; the middle half lies between them.
Unit price
Price per 100 g, per 100 ml or per item, so packs of different sizes can be compared.
Shrinkflation
A pack getting smaller while the price stays the same — a hidden price rise.
Hidden price increase
How much the price per gram or ml rose because the pack shrank.
Price basis
Whether a recorded shop price is per item or per kilogram.
Sale event
A dated platform sale such as Big Billion Days, Great Indian Festival, Prime Day or Myntra EORS.
Held-out listings
Products kept aside and never used for training, so accuracy is measured fairly.
Typical error
The median percentage gap between estimate and real price on held-out products.
R²
How much of the variation in prices the model explains, from 0 to 1.
Provenance
Whether a data row is real (observed) or synthetic (simulated).
Open Food Facts / Open Prices
Free, community-run databases of food products and shop prices (ODbL licence).

14Questions & troubleshooting

Is this telling me a seller is cheating?

No. Price Truth shows whether a price and discount look normal against history and a reference-price rule. It is a guide for shoppers, not proof of wrongdoing.

Are these live prices?

The catalogue prices are historical (Amazon January 2023, Flipkart 2015–16). Daily histories and cross-platform offers are simulated from those, calibrated to research and adjusted for inflation. Food lookups can be live. The Methods & data page lists exactly which parts are real and which are simulated.

Why does “Tomorrow's price” usually say “No forecast”?

Online prices change only every few days or weeks, so “same as today” is usually the best possible guess. The app shows a forecast only when a method actually does better than that on past days — otherwise it says so rather than inventing one.

Why does the discount check say “usual discount” for most products?

Outside sale periods most discounts are normal for the product. Inflated and real-drop verdicts appear mostly during sales. To try it, enter a much higher MRP.

“No product found for this barcode”

Open Food Facts does not know that barcode. Check the digits, or search by name instead.

“Live lookup is unavailable”

The internet connection or the Open Food Facts service is down. Switch on Saved responses only to use saved data.

My search finds nothing

Use fewer or more general words (e.g. “cable” rather than “braided usb-c fast charging cable”), and set Platform to Both.

My CSV import was rejected

The message names the problem. Common causes: a date in the future or not in YYYY-MM-DD form, a link that is not HTTPS, an empty variant, a negative or zero price, or a unit other than g, kg, ml, l or count.

Is my data stored?

No account is needed and nothing you enter is stored on a server or used for training. Observations stay in your browser session until you clear them or close the app; use Save my observations to keep a copy.
